one_liner: Nim port of a toy 500x500 ray tracer, timed at 130 ms vs 160 ms for the repo's GCC-built C and C++ ports.
what_it_does: A row from edin/raytracer, a 'performance comparison of various compilers' that ports one TypeScript sample ray tracer (a checkerboard plane, two shiny spheres, four lights, reflection depth 5) to about 25 languages; it is not a library. The Nim version (nim/RayTracer.nim, about 410 lines, rewritten in PR #4 'Copy cpp' in March 2021) renders the scene into a seq of BGRA pixels and writes a BMP. Using the result means writing your kernel in Nim; there is nothing to link into a C++ program.
how_it_is_fast: Two of the three sources of the gap are not language features. First, approximate math behind compile switches: -d:quake replaces sqrt plus divide in norm() (every primary ray, sphere normal and light vector) with a bit-trick inverse square root (magic 0x5fe6eb50c7b537a9) and one Newton step, and -d:intpow replaces libm pow(specular, 250.0 or 150.0) with exponentiation by squaring; the PR's own commit is titled 'add unfair optimizations'. Second, build flags: Nim's generated C got -march=native and LTO, while C was built with g++ -x c -O3 and C++ with -O2. Third, a leaner program: the scene lives in fixed-size arrays of a generic Scene[T, L: static int] with a variant (case) object per shape, so there is no virtual dispatch (the C++ port calls virtual GetIntersection/GetNormal/GetSurface and copies std::optional<Intersection>), the shadow test returns only a distance (C copies a full Intersection with its Ray per hit), and surface properties and the normalized reflection direction are computed once per hit (C computes surface properties twice per hit and re-normalizes the reflection direction for every unshadowed light).
when_to_use: As a template for fast scalar Nim code: compile-time-sized arrays, case objects instead of class hierarchies, and templates/macros for field-wise vector math compile to tight C with -d:danger.

As evidence that a naive C++ design (virtual calls per object, std::optional copies, -O2) leaves performance on the table: the PR #4 author measured the Nim rewrite without the math switches at 55 ms against 74 ms for the C++ port (hardware not stated).
Preview-quality rendering or geometry kernels where an inverse square root with about 0.2% error and integer-exponent pow are acceptable, if you copy the -d:quake and -d:intpow ideas consciously.
Small single-threaded CPU-bound programs where you already use Nim and want a reference point that its C backend is not a handicap.
when_not_to_use: As proof that Nim beats C or C++ as a language: the programs differ in algorithm (approximate norm, integer pow), work per hit and build flags, and the rows were measured about a year apart.
When output must match a reference image: with -d:quake the spheres come out slightly smaller than in the original Nim, C++ and D outputs (reported in issue #11).
As a renderer: three objects, four lights, no acceleration structure, no threads or SIMD, no API; it is a benchmark sample.
When you need a like-for-like comparison: no C build with -march=native and LTO, and no C++ build at -O3 with a switch-based design, has been timed in this repo.
For current-hardware numbers: the table is from an AMD FX-8120 and has not been re-measured since the June 2026 move to projects.xml.

integration.dependencies: Nim standard library only (math, times, macros, os, strutils); Nim's C backend compiler (GCC in the measured setup)
integration.min_toolchain: Not documented; the code dates from March 2021 (Nim 1.4 era) and was updated in June 2026; -d:lto needs a backend C compiler with LTO
integration.platforms: Any Nim target in principle; -march=native ties the binary to the build CPU and the quake trick assumes IEEE-754 binary64 layout

gotchas: Cross-run comparison: the C (GCC) and C++ (GCC) 160 ms rows first appear in the README of 1 May 2020 (commit 1ca4ffb, when Nim was listed at 1500 ms); the Nim row was set on 22 March 2021 after PR #4 (150 ms in 67da4de, then 130 ms in 8ea9877 the same day). The rows were never re-run together, compiler versions are not given, each is a single run rounded to 10 ms, and the three programs use different timers (Nim cpuTime, C clock(), C++ high_resolution_clock), all including scene setup.

The 130 ms build used -d:quake and -d:intpow (approximate inverse square root, integer pow) plus -march=native and LTO; the PR author labelled these 'unfair optimizations', and the current projects.xml drops -d:quake but keeps -d:intpow, -march=native and LTO for Nim while C stays at plain -O3 and C++ at -O2.

Latent bug in the Nim intersections template: in the plane branch, the closeness test (dist < closest) runs before dist is assigned, so it compares the default 0.0 and accepts any plane hit; this is harmless only because the plane is the first object in the scene, and reordering the scene would make the plane occlude nearer spheres.

The baselines have their own defects: the C Legalize() casts to uint8 before clamping, so channels above 1.0 overflow (undefined conversion) instead of saturating, and the README remark that the C++ port does bounds checking is not borne out by its source (no .at() calls).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among systems-and-safety siblings, the benchLANG Nim binary-trees entry measures Nim against C and C++ with matched -O3 -march=native -flto flags and the same algorithm on a dated 2026 run, so it is the stronger Nim data point; mosdepth and the c-blake tools (cligen/dents, procs, dups) are usable Nim programs that beat C tools, whereas this entry only shows that a carefully restructured Nim toy with approximate math beats an unoptimized C++ class-hierarchy port.
verified_claims_summary: The README table (single runs on an AMD FX-8120, apparently Windows with MinGW g++ given the run.bat scripts and MSVC rows) shows the 500x500 render at 130 ms for Nim built with -d:danger -d:lto -d:intpow -d:quake -march=native against 160 ms for C (g++ -x c -O3) and C++ (g++ -O2 -std=c++17), about 1.23x (derived from page data), with the C and C++ rows dating from May 2020 and the Nim row from March 2021. Third-party points in the repo agree on direction but not size: the PR #4 author measured 55 ms (no math switches) and 37 ms (with them) against 74 ms for C++ on unstated hardware, and jzakiya (issue #11) measured C/C++ at 75-78 ms against fast Nim at 42-45 ms on an i7-6700HQ.
status_note: MIT-licensed, 61 stars, last commit 2026-06-18 (a new projects.xml-driven 'ray' wrapper), but the results table has not been refreshed since 2021 and the Nim file is a benchmark sample, not a maintained component.
